Samuel H. Miller spent more than seven decades in Cleveland business and philanthropy, helping turn Forest City from a local lumber business into a national real estate developer while becoming one of the city’s most persistent builders of ties between its Jewish and Catholic communities.

Born in Cleveland in 1921, Miller was the son of poor Jewish immigrants and grew up speaking only Russian and Yiddish. As a child he peddled rags to neighborhood gas stations. He graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Western Reserve University in 1941 and attended Harvard Business School on a full scholarship, earning an MBA. He served in the U.S. Navy from 1942 to 1946, during the Second World War.

In 1947, Miller joined Forest City, then a local lumber and hardware business. He oversaw various areas of the company and played a key role in its evolution into a real estate firm and a nationally recognized commercial developer. He is particularly credited with spearheading Forest City’s move into land development. Miller became treasurer in 1992 and was named chairman of the board in 1993. In 1995, Albert B. Ratner joined him as co-chairman, and Miller later became co-chairman emeritus.

Miller became a nationally recognized leader in the Jewish community. He campaigned for the United Jewish Appeal across the United States, served on the board of the Jewish National Fund, and was named a Lifetime Honorary Trustee of the Jewish Community Federation of Cleveland.

His commitments were never confined to one community. In 1981 he began a relationship with Bishop Anthony M. Pilla, grounded in the conviction that Cleveland’s Jewish and Catholic communities needed to collaborate. Miller served on the board of the Catholic Diocese of Cleveland Foundation and led fundraising for inner-city Catholic schools. In 1993 he became the first Jewish recipient of the Archbishop Hoban award, and in 1995 he had an audience with Pope John Paul II. He was also a Lifetime Honorary Trustee of the National Conference of Christians and Jews.

The same breadth marked his civic service. Miller was a trustee of the Urban League, WVIZ, Crime Stoppers, the Police Memorial, and Medical Mutual of Ohio, and he took part in the Greater Cleveland Roundtable. In education, he served on the boards of Cleveland State University, Baldwin-Wallace College, Notre Dame College, and John Carroll University, and was an Honorary Trustee of Case Western Reserve University. At his alma mater he supported science enrichment programs for local high school students and endowed a large undergraduate scholarship fund; the western entrance to Adelbert Hall is named the Samuel H. Miller Plaza.

Health care was another lasting cause. Miller served on the board of directors and executive committee of The Cleveland Clinic, supported its cardiac care, and in 2003 was made a Distinguished Fellow of The Cleveland Clinic Foundation. The Clinic’s Maria and Sam Miller Emergency Services Building bears his name and his wife’s. He also gave to Playhouse Square and the Cleveland Orchestra.

His honors included the Ellis Island Medal of Honor, the American Red Cross National Humanitarian Award, a Lifetime Achievement Award from the Catholic Diocese of Cleveland in 2015, and a Lifetime Achievement Award from the *Cleveland Jewish News* in 2016. In 2013, he was inducted into the Cleveland International Hall of Fame.

Samuel H. Miller died on March 7, 2019, at age 97. He was survived by his wife, Maria, and four children.

His Cleveland legacy is visible in the company he helped build and in the institutions that carry his name. It is just as present in something harder to see: the working trust between the city’s Jewish and Catholic communities, which he spent decades insisting they needed, and helping them to keep.
